what_it_does: Serverless platforms (services like AWS Lambda where you upload a function and the cloud runs it on demand, spinning up a container — a lightweight isolated computing environment — for each request) suffer from 'cold starts': launching a new container from scratch takes hundreds of milliseconds, which is unacceptably slow. To avoid this, platforms keep recently-used containers alive in a warm pool, ready to handle the next matching request. The difficulty is that many requests arrive at the same time: the platform must decide whether to queue a new request and wait for an existing container to finish (a delayed warm start) or immediately spin up a cold new container. Existing policies ignore this concurrency dimension and make poor eviction choices (throwing away containers that are about to be needed again). CIDRE is an orchestration algorithm that looks at each container's current busyness and estimates when it will be free, then weighs that wait against the cold-start cost. Its eviction logic factors in both how recently a container was used and how likely it is to be needed again given current request concurrency, reducing unnecessary cold starts on real production workloads.
